title: Loving for others
hookLine: a friend's good news, a half-second pause, and a hadith that walks straight into it

lines: LOVE FOR HIM WHAT YOU LOVE.
cards: A friend gets the job you both applied for. Or the apartment. Or the news you've waited years to hear yourself.

The text arrives, and for some people there's a half-second before typing congratulations where something tightens. Nobody chooses that half-second. But a short hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari walks right into it.
The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: none of you truly believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself.

teach.h: YOUR OWN WANTING IS THE RULER.
teach.b: Look at how the sentence is built. It doesn't say: stop wanting good things. It starts from what a person already wants for himself: health, ease, being forgiven, a good name, rest.
Your own wanting is the ruler. Whatever you'd be glad to receive, want it for someone else too. Then the verb.
The hadith doesn't say give, or share, though those may follow.
It says love: yuhibbu, he loves. It's about what the heart wants. You can't always hand someone what they need.
You can always want it for them. Then who counts. The hadith in Bukhari says his brother.
A narration in Sahih Muslim gives the same words with his brother, or, the narrator adds, his neighbor. And a narration in al-Nasa'i spells out what kind of thing is meant: of good.
Not whatever you happen to crave, but the good: guidance, health, mercy, the thing that would actually help. And the strong opening: none of you believes.
Some commentators read this as faith not yet complete, not as a person leaving Islam.
The hadith points at a gap between believing in words and believing all the way down, and it finds that gap somewhere very ordinary: what happens inside when someone else gets the good thing.
The half-second is where the hadith does its work.

how: Muslims cite this hadith as a measure of faith: wanting for others the good one wants for oneself, and making du'a for others' good.

o: wanting for someone else the good you want for yourself
putting others' wishes always ahead of your own needs
giving away what you want so others can have it

games.q: loving for others — tap the pairs.
p: what a narration in al-Nasa'i adds

s: the hadith asks you to stop wanting good things for yourself
it starts from what you want for yourself and uses that as the measure for others.
the hadith's verb is love, not only give
yuhibbu, he loves: the heart's wanting comes first.
some commentators read 'none of you believes' as faith not yet complete
they read it as incomplete faith, not as leaving Islam.

games.q: your friend gets the very thing you were hoping for. the hadith in Bukhari gives you a measure for the next moment. what is it?
o: say nothing until the feeling passes.
want for them what you'd want for yourself.
point out it could just as easily have been you.
games.why: none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself: your own wanting becomes the measure for theirs.

practice: Name one thing you've been hoping for lately, rest, a good result, a door opening, and hold it a moment.
Then bring someone to mind, maybe the one whose good news stung a little, and picture them receiving that same thing, staying with it until the wanting feels real, or at least a little closer.
If you pray, you can ask for it for them by name, before you ask for yourself.

wordCard.voice: Loving for others. From the hadith in Bukhari: wanting for another person the good you want for yourself, as part of faith itself. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: he loves. the verb at the heart of the hadith (Bukhari 13).

carryVoice: Your line: love it for them. Your own wanting is the ruler. Tomorrow, contentment with little.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 13 (none of you believes until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself)
Sahih Muslim 45 (for his brother, or for his neighbor)
Sunan al-Nasa'i 5017 (what he loves for himself of good)
